# RFC 8030 (message retention) vs RFC 8291 (content encryption) — source-backed comparison

Primary sources (both fetched in full from rfc-editor.org on 2026-10-24):
- RFC 8030, "Generic Event Delivery Using HTTP Push" (Thomson, Damaggio, Raymor; Dec 2016): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8030.txt
- RFC 8291, "Message Encryption for Web Push" (Thomson; Nov 2017): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8291.txt

## 1. RFC 8030 — retention / short-term storage (delivery mechanism)

What it provides:
- TTL header: the application server MUST include TTL (seconds) in every push request; the push service MUST return 400 if TTL is omitted (RFC 8030 §5.2).
- The push service stores the message so it can be delivered when the intermittently connected user agent resumes monitoring: "User agents are often only intermittently connected, and so benefit from having short-term message storage at the push service" (§5.2). Stored undelivered messages are delivered when the user agent recommences monitoring (§7.2).
- After TTL elapses, the push service MUST NOT attempt delivery (§5.2). Zero-TTL messages are delivered immediately if the UA is available; if the UA is unavailable they expire and are never delivered (§5.2).
- Replacement via Topic header lets a stored message be replaced while the UA is offline (§5.4).
- Acknowledgement: the user agent MUST DELETE the push message resource for at-least-once delivery; the service SHOULD retry until the advertised expiration (§6.2). Receipts (§5.1, §6.3) are service→app-server confirmations of acknowledgement.

What it does NOT guarantee (per the independent review, corrected wording):
- Retention is best-effort, not a guarantee of the requested duration. The service MAY retain a message for a shorter duration than requested, indicating the actual TTL in its response (§5.2); it MAY later expire a message before its advertised TTL (§7.2); it is "not obligated to store messages indefinitely" (§7.2); it MAY cease retrying delivery before expiration (§6.2). So: short-term storage improves delivery reliability for offline UAs, but no fixed retention duration is guaranteed.
- A 201/202 response only means the push service accepted the message: "This does not indicate that the message was delivered to the user agent" (§5). An accepted push does NOT prove a physical phone received it. Only a 204 receipt (§6.3) confirms the UA acknowledged — and even that is an acknowledgement by the user-agent software, not proof the human saw it.
- TLS protects messages only from external parties; the push service can inspect and modify content (§8, §8.1).

## 2. RFC 8291 — content encryption (payload protection)

What it provides:
- End-to-end confidentiality, integrity and data-origin authentication between application server and user agent, hiding content from the push service (Abstract, §1, §2).
- Mechanism: ECDH on P-256 between UA and app server, a 16-octet authentication secret from the UA, HKDF (SHA-256) combining them, then AES128-GCM via the "aes128gcm" encrypted content encoding of RFC 8188 (§2, §3, §3.1–3.4). Per-message ECDH key pair and random salt from the app server (§2).
- Single record per message; padding delimiter 0x02 MUST be checked (§4).

What it does NOT guarantee (per the independent review, corrected wording):
- Size: RFC 8291 §4 states a push service "is not required to support more than 4096 octets of payload body" (referring to RFC 8030 §7.2, where services MUST NOT return 413 for bodies ≤4096 bytes). This yields at most 3993 octets of plaintext (4096 − 86 header − 1 padding − 16 AEAD tag). That is a minimum interoperability floor, not a universal protocol maximum; services may accept larger payloads.
- Metadata: timing, length (unless padded), and which app server talks to which UA/subscription remain visible to the push service (§7). No HTTP header fields are protected by the content encoding (§7).
- It does not itself provide delivery, storage, or receipts — it only protects payload content while the message sits at and transits the push service.

## 3. How they relate

- Orthogonal layers of the same system: RFC 8030 defines transport, subscription, TTL-based retention and receipts; RFC 8291 encrypts the body that RFC 8030 carries. RFC 8030 §8.1 requires applications to use end-to-end confidentiality and names [ENCRYPT] (RFC 8291) as the W3C Push API's adopted mechanism; RFC 8291 §1 explicitly builds on RFC 8030 and its UA/push-service/app-server roles.
- Encryption is independent of retention: an encrypted message stored at the push service stays unreadable to the service for the whole retention window; retention duration and encryption strength are unrelated guarantees.

## 4. Relation to an offline mobile device

- Offline device: RFC 8030 §5.2/§7.2 — the push service stores the message for the TTL (which it may shorten, §5.2/§7.2) and delivers it when the device resumes monitoring. If TTL is zero or expires first, the message is never delivered (§5.2, §7.2).
- The device's radio/battery motivation for consolidated push is described in RFC 8030 §1 and Urgency (§5.3).
- Encryption (RFC 8291) matters while offline because the ciphertext is stored server-side; the service never sees plaintext. Key agreement happens at subscription time (§2.1), so decryption works whenever the device comes back online — within the TTL window.
- Critical caveat: a 201/202 from the push service (§5, §5.1) proves only that the service accepted the message for delivery; it does not prove the physical phone received it. Only a 204 receipt after the UA's DELETE acknowledgement (§6.2, §6.3) indicates delivery to the user agent — and even then the service MAY stop retrying early (§6.2), and a zero-TTL message may be removed before any acknowledgement is possible (§5.2).

## 5. Corrections from the independent review (both supported by the primary text)

1. Guarantee wording: RFC 8030 §5.2 and §7.2 explicitly allow shorter retention and early expiry, so retention is described here as best-effort short-term storage, not a guarantee of the requested TTL duration.
2. Size wording: RFC 8291 §4 gives a minimum supported 4096-octet payload body (3993-octet plaintext capacity), not a universal protocol maximum.

note: Scoped standards comparison with actual source reads; factual review and all other real-world gates remain separate.
